strengths: Strong and extensive empirical evaluation: xRFM is benchmarked on TALENT (300 datasets, 31 methods), TabArena-Lite (with Elo/inference-time Pareto analysis), and large meta-test datasets up to 500k samples, against strong baselines including GBDTs (XGBoost, CatBoost, LightGBM), RealMLP, ModernNCA, and TabPFN-v2.

The core idea is well-motivated and clearly articulated: combining AGOP-based feature learning (RFM) with an adaptive tree structure enables local feature learning for hierarchical tabular structure while achieving log-linear training and logarithmic inference scaling — addressing both known limitations of kernel machines (no feature learning, poor scaling).

The synthetic example (Fig. 2) cleanly demonstrates the local feature learning benefit over standard kernel RFM, and the interpretability section (Fig. 7) provides native AGOP-based feature importance across multiple real datasets, including heterogeneous features across leaves.

Honest reporting of limitations: the paper does not claim SOTA on classification, discusses fairness of hyperparameter search budgets, and provides hyperparameter search spaces and detailed algorithms (A.1–A.5) in the appendix.
Code release with a scikit-learn-style API improves reproducibility, and the method is very fast at inference (orders of magnitude faster than many baselines).
weaknesses: Limited algorithmic novelty: the method is a combination of existing kernel-RFM (Radhakrishnan et al.) with tree-based data partitioning; tree routing of models to data subsets is conceptually similar to TabPFN-v2's random-forest leaf routing, and the AGOP reuse from RFM is incremental. The contribution is more of a strong engineering + benchmarking effort than a fundamentally new method.

Ablations are incomplete. Key design choices are not systematically ablated: sensitivity to the split-model subsample size m, the effect of one RFM iteration vs. more in the split model, leaf size C, and a direct comparison against simpler splitting criteria (e.g., splitting on the single most important coordinate as in trees, or gradient-based single-feature splits) beyond a brief mention that unsupervised splits underperform.

The interpretability evaluation is qualitative and anecdotal (four datasets); there is no quantitative comparison with established interpretability methods (SHAP, permutation importance, tree feature importances), and the paper itself acknowledges this as future work. Claims of 'native interpretability' as a headline benefit are stronger than the evidence provided.

Comparison fairness concerns: xRFM receives substantial hyperparameter tuning (100+ trials with wide search spaces, e.g., kernel exponents, bandwidth, diagonal vs. full AGOP, adaptive bandwidth), while some baselines rely on default or less-tuned configurations; TabPFN-v2 is subsampled to 10k samples and excluded from some runtime comparisons, which may bias results in xRFM's favor on regression.
Memory/model-size costs of xRFM are not discussed: storing per-leaf kernel coefficients and split vectors for up to 500k samples could be substantial, which matters for the scalability claims.

Classification performance is not best-in-class (third-ranked on TALENT classification, behind TabPFN-v2/RealMLP), which weakens the 'accurate at all scales and tasks' framing; the headline claim rests mainly on regression.

No theoretical analysis of the tree-partitioning procedure (e.g., when AGOP-top-eigenvector splits recover relevant subspaces, or effect of splitting on prediction error bounds); the O(n log n) claim is only empirical/structural.

Writing issues: duplicated numbering in the Discussion ('(1)' twice), vague URL placeholders in the abstract and appendix, and some overstated phrasing ('essentially unlimited amounts of training data').

strengths: Clear and well-motivated combination of two ideas: feature-learning kernel machines (RFM/AGOP) and adaptive tree-based data partitioning, yielding local feature learning, O(n log n) training and O(log n) inference.

Extensive empirical evaluation across three established benchmarks (TALENT, TabArena-Lite, meta-test) against a large number of strong baselines (GBDTs, RealMLP, TabPFN-v2, TabM, ModernNCA), with best performance on 100 TALENT regression datasets and competitive results on classification, plus Pareto-frontier analysis of accuracy vs. inference time.

Native interpretability via AGOP diagonal entries and top eigenvectors, demonstrated on synthetic data (Fig. 2) and several real datasets with plausible domain-consistent findings (California housing, Covertype, taxi tipping, breast cancer).
Complete algorithmic specification (Algorithms A.1-A.5), hyperparameter search spaces (Table A.1), and released code with a scikit-learn-style API, supporting reproducibility.
Statistical support for key claims (Wilcoxon tests vs. KRR and RFM; Elo and multiple aggregation metrics).
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty: the core components (kernel-RFM from Radhakrishnan et al., AGOP, tree partitioning, median splits) are existing ideas; the contribution is largely an engineering combination plus incremental kernel/AGOP variants, which weakens the theoretical contribution expected at a top-tier venue.

No theoretical analysis: claims about scaling (O(n log n) training, O(log n) inference) and the benefits of local feature learning are supported only by a single synthetic example, not by formal results or broader empirical validation of when/why local feature learning helps.

Classification results are not state-of-the-art (third-ranked on TALENT classification; behind TabPFN-v2, RealMLP, CatBoost on TabArena-Lite), so the 'best-in-class' narrative rests mainly on regression.

Heavy hyperparameter tuning burden: the search space (bandwidth, exponents, kernel type, diagonal/adaptive options, regularization) is substantial and per-configuration training time comparisons may understate total compute; the effect of tuning budget on the reported advantage is not analyzed.

Interpretability claims are not rigorously evaluated: no quantitative comparison against established interpretability methods (Shapley values, tree feature importances, gradient-based scores), which the authors themselves acknowledge as future work; interpretability findings are anecdotal.

Some ablations are asserted rather than shown: e.g., 'we found that splitting in this manner outperformed splits based on unsupervised approaches' is stated without results, and there is no sensitivity analysis for leaf size C or the number of split-model samples m.

The meta-test comparison mixes results computed by the authors with numbers reported in the literature, and the 'essentially unlimited data' claim in the abstract overstates what is demonstrated (max ~500K samples).

strengths: Clear and well-motivated contribution: combining feature-learning kernel machines (RFM) with an adaptive, AGOP-guided tree partitioning is a sensible and novel way to obtain local feature learning while scaling kernel methods to large tabular datasets.

Unusually thorough empirical evaluation: results across three benchmarks (TALENT with 300 datasets and 31 baselines, TabArena-Lite with Elo/runtime tradeoffs, and meta-test datasets with 70k-500k samples), covering regression, binary, and multiclass settings, with strong baselines including XGBoost/CatBoost/LightGBM, RealMLP, ModernNCA, and TabPFN-v2.

Scalability claims are supported with runtime analysis (Fig. 5, B.1) showing the expected super-linear-to-log-linear transition and competitive or superior training/inference times relative to GBDTs and neural methods.

Native interpretability is a genuine differentiator: AGOP diagonals and top eigenvectors are used to expose features and local heterogeneity (Fig. 7), with the synthetic example (Fig. 2) cleanly demonstrating the benefit of local over global feature learning.

Statistical rigor where possible: Wilcoxon significance tests against KRR and standard RFM (Fig. 4), multiple aggregation metrics (SGM, arithmetic mean, normalized scores), and detailed reporting of per-dataset ranks and Top-X percentages in the appendix.
Reproducibility: full hyperparameter search spaces (Table A.1), detailed pseudocode (Algorithms A.1-A.5), data preprocessing details, and public scikit-learn-style code.
weaknesses: The method is largely an assembly of known components (RFM, median tree splits, kernel tuning); there is no theoretical analysis of the resulting estimator (e.g., when local AGOP splits help, generalization or consistency properties), which limits conceptual depth beyond engineering.

Performance is lopsided: xRFM is clearly best on regression, but only third-ranked on classification, and it falls notably behind RealMLP/TabR on multiclass tasks with >10 classes (Table B.3); the 'competitive with the best' framing slightly overstates classification results.

Comparison fairness concerns: TabPFN-v2 is subsampled to 10,000 samples and excluded from some runtime comparisons, while xRFM receives a large, benchmark-specific hyperparameter search; the sensitivity of conclusions to these choices is not analyzed.
No uncertainty quantification on the headline aggregate metrics (e.g., variability over benchmark subsets or seeds), and the shifted geometric mean can be sensitive to the epsilon choice.

The interpretability claims are qualitative only: AGOP-based feature importance is compared to intuitive expectations on four datasets but not quantitatively benchmarked against SHAP, gradient-based, or tree-based importance measures, which the authors themselves acknowledge as future work.

Minor presentation issues: duplicate enumeration in the Discussion ('(1)... and (1)...'), a truncated code URL in the abstract, and some memory-footprint implications of storing data and models at every leaf are not discussed.

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three established benchmarks (TALENT with 300 datasets, TabArena-Lite, and the meta-test benchmark with large datasets up to 500k samples), covering both regression and classification against 31 methods including GBDTs, tuned neural networks, and tabular foundation models (TabPFN-v2)

Clear, concrete headline result: xRFM is the best method on TALENT regression by all aggregation metrics and sits on the empirical Pareto frontier of performance vs. inference time, addressing the well-known scalability limitation of kernel machines (O(n log n) training, O(log n) inference)

The method is well-motivated: combining feature-learning kernel machines (RFM) with supervised tree partitioning enables local feature learning, demonstrated convincingly on a synthetic task (Fig. 2) where splits recover heterogeneous feature relevance

Native interpretability through the AGOP (diagonal feature importance, top eigenvector analysis) is demonstrated on multiple real datasets with sensible, interpretable findings, with no post-hoc tooling required

Good ablation and sensitivity analysis: comparison of split methods (AGOP vs. PCA vs. random forest), temperature-tuned ensembling, comparisons against kernel ridge regression and vanilla RFM with statistical testing (Wilcoxon, p < 1e-4), meta-feature analysis, and portfolio experiments

Algorithmic details are thorough (full pseudocode for tree partitioning, routing, training, inference; complete hyperparameter search spaces in Table A.1), and code with a scikit-learn-style API is released, supporting reproducibility

Honest and careful positioning: the paper discusses when xRFM is only 'competitive' rather than best (classification), clarifies the use of the 'Lite' TabArena version, and explicitly discusses related scaling approaches (Nystrom, Falkon, EigenPro)
weaknesses: Conceptual novelty is moderate: the core idea is a combination of existing components (kernel-RFM from Radhakrishnan et al. 2024 plus tree-based data partitioning), with the contribution being primarily engineering refinements (Lp,q kernels, diagonal-AGOP option, categorical precomputation, adaptive bandwidth) rather than a new learning principle; there is no theoretical analysis of the tree partitioning (e.g., consistency, approximation error of the split procedure)

On classification, xRFM is only third-ranked behind TabPFN-v2 and RealMLP on multiclass tasks and does not dominate; the claim of being state-of-the-art on tabular data is thus task-dependent and should be tempered

Interpretability claims are largely anecdotal: AGOP feature importances are shown to be 'sensible' on a handful of datasets, but there is no rigorous validation against established attribution methods (Shapley values, permutation importance) or controlled ground-truth experiments beyond one synthetic example

Some fairness concerns in the runtime comparisons: xRFM's inference time is naturally tiny because a single tree is traversed, whereas GBDT ensembles perform many tree traversals; also, comparisons on meta-test rely on literature-reported baseline numbers, and hyperparameter search budgets for the baselines are not fully controlled in all settings

Robustness of the method is underexplored with respect to its own key hyperparameters (leaf size C, split subsample size m): only one leaf size (60k) is used in the main benchmarks, and the paper itself notes the leaf-size/performance tradeoff as future work

The soft-routing/temperature-tuning variant improves error but is relegated to the appendix; the headline results use hard routing, and the practical guidance for when ensembling is needed is not clear

Potential memory/storage cost of storing per-leaf kernel models and split directions for very large datasets is not discussed, and the 'essentially unlimited data' claim, while supported by log-linear scaling, is somewhat stronger than the evidence (largest experiment is 500k samples / 10M rows in one dataset)

strengths: Comprehensive empirical evaluation across three established tabular benchmarks (TALENT with 300 datasets, TabArena-Lite, and the meta-test benchmark with large datasets up to 500k samples), with 31 competing methods including TabPFN-v2, GBDT variants, and strong neural baselines.

Strong headline results: xRFM is the best method on TALENT regression across all aggregation metrics and is competitive on classification, with statistical testing (Wilcoxon) supporting comparisons against KRR and RFM.

The core idea of combining tree-based data partitioning with feature-learning kernel machines (leaf RFMs) is sensible and clearly motivated: it enables local feature learning and log-linear training / logarithmic inference time, addressing the well-known scalability limits of kernel machines.

The interpretability angle via the AGOP (diagonal feature importances and top eigenvector analysis) is natively supported by the model rather than post-hoc, and is illustrated on synthetic data (Fig. 2) plus several real datasets with plausible, domain-consistent findings.

Full algorithmic details are provided (Algorithms A.1-A.5), hyperparameter search spaces are documented (Table A.1), ablations on split methods and ensembling are included (Appendix B, Tables E.1-E.2), and code with a scikit-learn-style API is released, supporting reproducibility.
Useful practical analyses: runtime scaling behavior (Fig. 5, F.2), meta-feature analysis (Appendix C), and portfolio/ensembling experiments (Appendix D).
weaknesses: Algorithmic novelty is moderate: the method is essentially a tree of RFM models, combining the existing RFM algorithm (Radhakrishnan et al., 2024) with tree partitioning, similar in spirit to the TabPFN-v2 random-forest routing they themselves cite (Hollmann et al., 2025). The main contribution is empirical rather than conceptual.

The theoretical complexity claims are not rigorously established: O(n log n) training and O(log n) inference are asserted informally, but the split model fitting cost, AGOP computation, and kernel evaluations per node (each leaf RFM is still super-quadratic in leaf size, up to 60,000 samples) are not carefully accounted for; a formal analysis would strengthen the claims.

Interpretability claims are only weakly validated: the AGOP-based feature importance is never compared against established methods (Shapley values, permutation importance, tree-based importance), as acknowledged in the Discussion. The case studies are anecdotal; there is no quantitative faithfulness or sanity-check evaluation (e.g., on synthetic data with known ground truth beyond the single Fig. 2 example).

Some claims overstate the evidence: 'competitive to the best methods across 200 classification datasets' masks weaker results in several sub-tables (e.g., rank 5.46 and 8.75 on multiclass/binary subsets in Tables E.5/E.6, second to TabPFN-v2 in several settings), and the 'best performance' claim relies on specific aggregation metrics (shifted geometric mean) whose sensitivity is not discussed.

Hyperparameter search appears extensive (hundreds of configurations implied by the search space in Table A.1) while details on how many random configurations, tuning budget, and number of CV folds were used for xRFM versus baselines are thin; potential tuning-budget asymmetries could inflate reported wins, particularly given the meta-feature analysis admits cross-validation/tuning differences between benchmarks.
The Table A.1 search space description contains inconsistencies/typos (e.g., 'p ∈ U(0.7, 1.4) and p ∈ {q, 2}', exponent q vs. p usage is confusing), which hurts clarity of the experimental protocol.

No ablations on key design choices such as the leaf size C (60,000 is fixed), the number of split-model samples, and the sensitivity of results to the median-split scheme; the tradeoff between leaf size and performance is explicitly left as future work.

Ethical/societal impact of the medical-flavored interpretability analysis (breast cancer case study) is not discussed; interpretability conclusions drawn from AGOP entries on clinical data without validation could be misleading in practice.

strengths: The paper addresses a timely and important problem: developing scalable, accurate, and interpretable models for tabular data where GBDTs still dominate.

The core idea — combining feature-learning kernel machines (RFM/AGOP) with adaptive, supervised tree-based data partitioning — is well motivated: it enables local feature learning on subpopulations and yields O(n log n) training / O(log n) inference, addressing the well-known scalability ceiling of kernel methods.

Empirical evaluation is extensive and multi-benchmark: TALENT (100 regression, 200 classification datasets, 31 baselines including TabPFN-v2, RealMLP, CatBoost/XGBoost), TabArena-Lite with Elo and inference-time Pareto analysis, and the meta-test benchmark up to 500k samples where direct kernel solvers are intractable. xRFM is best on TALENT regression across all aggregation metrics and beats KRR/standard RFM with statistical significance (Wilcoxon p < 1e-4).

The paper is honest about mixed results: it clearly reports that xRFM is only third on classification and near (not on) the Pareto frontier there, and the meta-feature analysis (Appendix C) probes dataset-selection effects rather than cherry-picking.
Useful ablations: split-method comparison (AGOP vs. PCA vs. RF importance, Tables E.1-E.2), temperature-tuned soft routing, scaling behavior (Fig. 5, F.2), and portfolio experiments with GBDTs.

Natively interpretable predictions via per-leaf AGOPs is a genuine differentiator over GBDTs/TabPFN; the synthetic example (Fig. 2) cleanly demonstrates local feature learning that global RFM cannot capture, and case studies on real data (California housing, taxi tipping, breast cancer) yield sensible features consistent with the literature.

Reproducibility is strong: complete algorithmic pseudocode (Algs. A.1-A.5), full hyperparameter search spaces (Table A.1), details on baselines and preprocessing, and released scikit-learn-style code.
weaknesses: Novelty is somewhat incremental: the paper is essentially (existing) kernel-RFM + tree partitioning + hyperparameter engineering. There is no theoretical analysis of the tree-splitting procedure (e.g., consistency, when AGOP-based splits recover the true hierarchical structure), no convergence or approximation guarantees, and the technical machinery is largely assembled from prior work.

The interpretability claims are under-evaluated: AGOP-based importance is demonstrated on only four datasets with qualitative, anecdotal validation. There is no quantitative comparison against established interpretability tools (SHAP, permutation importance, gradient-based scores), which the authors themselves acknowledge as future work; claims that AGOP explanations are trustworthy therefore exceed the evidence.

Classification results are weaker than the abstract framing suggests: xRFM is third on TALENT classification, trails TabPFN-v2 substantially in binary/multiclass on TabArena-Lite (Elo 1310 vs. 1419/1313 tuned), and its default configuration is mid-pack (Elo 943-1129). The strong regression advantage does not carry over.

Benchmark fairness concerns: TabPFN-v2 is subsampled to 10k samples and restricted to <=10 classes on TALENT, potentially underestimating its performance relative to xRFM; on meta-test, xRFM results are partly compared against literature-reported numbers rather than a controlled rerun, and the xRFM hyperparameter search was adjusted per benchmark, which raises questions about tuning-budget parity.

Scalability claims are overstated: leaves are capped at 60k samples with exact solvers, and training cost is super-linear up to ~60k samples (Fig. 5); 'essentially unlimited' data sizes are not demonstrated (max ~500k, single-GPU). Runtime comparisons on TALENT also involve a 100x tuning-overhead caveat that complicates the 'fastest method' claim.

Several design choices feel heuristic and under-justified (e.g., p sampled uniformly from U(0.7,1.4), the 80/20 kernel-type split, the temperature-tuning weights with top-8 leaf ensemble), making the method somewhat fragile and its success partly attributable to extensive tuning per benchmark.
